title: THE UNTOLD STORY OF ABNER
paragraphs:
THE UNTOLD STORY OF ABNER
The Kingmaker Who Never Wore the Crown, the Warrior Who Died at the Gate, and the Tragedy of a Man Who Came Too Late
There are names in Scripture that echo through history.
And then there are names buried beneath the shadows of greater men.
Names most believers have read but never truly met.
His story is not merely a historical footnote tucked between the rise of Saul and the reign of David.
His story is the story of countless people sitting in church pews today.
People who spent years defending the wrong kingdom.
People who knew the truth but delayed surrender.
People who finally moved toward God's will only to discover how much had already been lost.
Because Abner may have been one of the most gifted men in Israel.
Yet history remembers him not as a king.
But as a man who almost got there.
And "almost" is one of the saddest words in the Bible.
The first time we meet Abner, he is introduced as Saul's military commander.
Yet throughout much of his life, Abner would use his gifts to defend a kingdom God had already rejected.
That is where the tragedy begins.
Because talent without surrender can become a weapon against God's purposes.
To understand Abner, you must understand Saul.
Saul had been chosen by God.
Eventually the prophet Samuel delivered one of the most devastating declarations in Scripture:
"The LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you today and has given it to a neighbor of yours, who is better than you."
The crown was still on Saul's head.
But heaven had already moved on.
The future king was already walking the earth.
Yet Abner stayed loyal to Saul.
Not because he didn't know David existed.
But because loyalty can become dangerous when it is attached to something God is no longer blessing.
Many people are living there right now.
Defending relationships God told them to leave.
Protecting habits God told them to surrender.
Building kingdoms God never asked them to build.
You can be faithful to the wrong thing.
When Saul died at the battle of Gilboa, everything changed.
The kingdom should have transitioned to David.
Instead, he took Saul's surviving son Ish-bosheth and installed him as king.
David, God's chosen king, was waiting.
Yet Abner placed his strength behind a man literally remembered as "Man of Shame."
Because one powerful man refused to align himself with what God had already declared.
A gifted person moving against God's direction can create damage far beyond themselves.
Entire generations can suffer from delayed obedience.
Then comes one of the most fascinating moments in Abner's life.
Eventually tension erupted between Abner and Ish-bosheth.
The king accused Abner of taking one of Saul's concubines.
Whether true or false, the accusation infuriated him.
And for the first time, he openly acknowledged what he had known all along.
"The LORD has sworn to David that He would transfer the kingdom from the house of Saul and establish the throne of David."
Yet he continued fighting against God's revealed will.
How many people are doing the same thing?
Abner's greatest problem was never ignorance.
At last, Abner decided to act.
He promised to unite Israel under God's chosen king.
For the first time in years, Abner moved toward the purpose of God.
This is one of the most beautiful moments in Scripture.
Because God's kingdom has room for repentant enemies.
The Gospel shines through this moment.
Jesus receives people who spent years running from Him.
Yet when they come, He welcomes them.
Years earlier Abner had killed Joab's brother Asahel during battle.
Then Scripture records one of the most chilling scenes in Israel's history.
"Joab took him aside into the midst of the gate as if to speak privately with him, and there struck him in the stomach."
The place where he should have entered a new future.
The place where reconciliation should have begun.
The place where his greatest chapter should have started.
He publicly honored the fallen commander.
"Should Abner die as a fool dies?"
"Should Abner die the death of a fool?"
Yet even wise men can make tragic decisions.
This is where the story reaches into our lives.
Many people imagine rebellion looks like shaking your fist at heaven.
After I enjoy sin a little longer.
After I finish building my own plans.
You do not control how long the gate stays open.
The opportunity God gives today is not guaranteed tomorrow.

Abner finally stepped into his kairos moment.
But years of resistance had already created consequences he could not escape.
That does not mean God stopped loving him.
It means delayed obedience is never free.
Perhaps that is why Abner's story lingers long after the chapter ends.
Because most people are not Saul.
They know what needs to change.
They know where repentance is needed.
They know where surrender is overdue.
They know which kingdom they have been defending.
And they know which King truly deserves their loyalty.
The question is whether they will respond before another year passes.
"Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand."
The Greek word for repent is:
To change one's mind so deeply that it changes the direction of one's life.
That is exactly what Abner finally did.
But Scripture leaves us wondering what might have happened if he had done it sooner.
How much bloodshed could have been avoided?
How many lives could have been spared?
How much peace could have been experienced?
Maybe that is the true untold story of Abner.
Not the story of how he died.
But the story of how long he waited to live.
And perhaps someone reading this has recognized themselves in him.
The saddest tragedy is not dying before your time—it is arriving at God's truth years after you could have been walking in it.
